1.title: Scheduling and Scaling
1.text: Welcome to Module 5: Scheduling and Scaling. This module is in the Kubernetes Fundamentals domain, and it covers the topic called Scheduling. By the end you will be able to do four things. Explain how the scheduler filters, scores and binds. Place Pods with node selectors, affinity, taints, tolerations and spread constraints. Use priority, Q O S classes and eviction order in a scenario. And compare the H P A, the V P A, the Cluster Autoscaler and KEDA.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Sells More at the Weekend
1.text: At Harbor Books, the weekend brings many more visitors, and the storefront must keep up. Payment Pods should run on dedicated nodes, and the replicas should be spread so that one failure does not take the shop down. Checkout matters more than the nightly report if the cluster is full. In this module you control where Pods go, and how many there are.

1.title: How the Scheduler Decides: Filter, Score, Bind
1.text: The kube scheduler watches for new Pods with no node. Filtering removes nodes that cannot run the Pod, for example nodes without enough free resources for its requests. Scoring ranks the remaining nodes, and the highest score wins. Binding records the choice with the A P I server. If no node is feasible, the Pod stays unscheduled, shown as Pending. The diagram shows five nodes becoming three after filtering. Exam tip: filter removes, score ranks, bind records.

1.title: nodeSelector and Node Affinity
1.text: A node selector is the simplest way to pick nodes. The Pod runs only on nodes whose labels match. Node affinity is more expressive, with operators such as In, Not In, Exists and Does Not Exist. A required rule is hard. A preferred rule is soft, and the scheduler only tries to meet it. If you set both a node selector and node affinity, both must be satisfied. The snippet asks for nodes with an S S D disk, in one of two zones. Exam tip: required means must, and preferred means try.

1.title: Pod Affinity and Anti-Affinity
1.text: Pod affinity places a Pod in a domain that already runs Pods with matching labels. Pod anti-affinity keeps it out of such a domain, for example to spread replicas over nodes. The topology key, a node label, defines the domain: a node, a rack or a zone. These rules look at other Pods' labels, not at node labels, and they cost scheduling time in large clusters. Exam tip: node affinity reads node labels, and Pod affinity reads Pod labels.

1.title: Taints and Tolerations
1.text: A taint on a node repels Pods. A toleration on a Pod lets it be placed on a matching tainted node. A toleration allows placement, but it does not guarantee it. The effect decides how strict the taint is. No Schedule means no new Pods without a toleration, and running Pods stay. Prefer No Schedule is the soft version. And No Execute also evicts running Pods that do not tolerate the taint. Exam tip: taints repel, tolerations permit, and No Execute is the only effect that evicts.

1.title: Topology Spread Constraints
1.text: Topology spread constraints spread Pods across failure domains, such as zones and nodes. Max skew is the largest permitted difference in matching Pods between a domain and the domain with the fewest. The topology key names the node label that defines the domains, and the label selector says which Pods count. When unsatisfiable chooses between Do Not Schedule, which is hard, and Schedule Anyway, which is soft. In the diagram, three zones hold two, two and one Pods, so the next Pod goes to the third zone. Exam tip: use spread constraints for even distribution, and anti-affinity to keep Pods apart.

1.title: Priority and Preemption
1.text: A Priority Class maps a name to an integer. The higher the value, the more important the Pod. A Pod picks one with priority class name. When a Pod finds no room, the scheduler may preempt: it evicts lower priority Pods to make space. Preemption policy Never stops a Pod from preempting others. Values for your own classes go up to one billion. Larger ones are reserved for system cluster critical and system node critical. Exam tip: priority decides who is evicted to make room, not where a Pod goes.

1.title: QoS Classes and Eviction
1.text: Kubernetes assigns every Pod a Q O S class, from its requests and limits. Guaranteed means every container has C P U and memory requests and limits, and each limit equals its request. Burstable means the Pod is not Guaranteed, but at least one request or limit is set. Best Effort means no container has any request or limit. When a node runs out of resources, the kube let evicts Best Effort Pods first, then Burstable, and Guaranteed last. The kube let itself ranks by usage above requests and by priority, so the Q O S order is the likely result. Exam tip: no requests and limits means first to go.

1.title: Static Pods and Manual Placement
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. A static Pod is a Pod that the kube let runs on one node, from manifest files in a folder. The A P I server does not manage it, but the kube let shows a mirror Pod there. The other mechanism is node name, a field that names the node for a Pod directly and skips the scheduler. It is unusual. The main use of static Pods is a self-hosted control plane. Exam tip: static Pods belong to one kube let, not to a controller.

1.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
1.text: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, the H P A, changes the number of Pods of a Deployment or Stateful Set to match demand. It compares a metric, such as average C P U utilization, with a target. Utilization is measured against the Pods' requests, so with no requests set, it takes no action. Metrics come from the Metrics Server, and the H P A checks about every fifteen seconds. Min replicas and max replicas bound the result. The snippet targets sixty percent C P U for the storefront. Exam tip: the H P A scales out and in, and it needs C P U requests to work.

2.title: Other Autoscalers: VPA, Cluster Autoscaler and KEDA
2.text: This slide is tagged archived topic. The H P A adds or removes Pods. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler, the V P A, makes Pods bigger or smaller, by setting requests from observed usage. The Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled, and removes nodes that stay underutilized. KEDA, Kubernetes Event Driven Autoscaling, scales workloads from events. And the Metrics Server feeds the H P A and the V P A. Exam tip: Pods out, Pods up, nodes out: H P A, V P A, Cluster Autoscaler.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Scheduling
2.text: Six pairs to keep apart. Filter or score: filtering removes nodes that cannot run the Pod, and scoring ranks the rest. Affinity or taint: affinity attracts, taints repel, and tolerations permit. No Schedule or No Execute: No Schedule blocks new Pods, and No Execute also evicts running ones. Requests or limits: requests drive placement, and limits are enforced. Q O S order: Best Effort is evicted first, and Guaranteed last. And H P A, V P A or Cluster Autoscaler: more Pods, bigger Pods, or more nodes. Exam tip: ask whether the rule attracts, repels, spreads or ranks.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: To recap. The scheduler filters, scores and binds, and if no node is feasible the Pod stays Pending. Node selectors and node affinity use node labels, and Pod affinity uses Pod labels. Taints repel, tolerations permit, and spread constraints even out zones. Higher priority can preempt lower priority, and Best Effort Pods are evicted first. Static Pods run from manifest files under one kube let. And autoscaling: the H P A scales Pods out and in, the V P A resizes Pods, the Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes, and KEDA scales on events. Now nine practice questions.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. In which order does the kube scheduler carry out its main steps for a new Pod? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The scheduler filters out nodes that cannot run the Pod, scores the feasible ones, and then binds the Pod to the highest scoring node by telling the A P I server. Binding comes last.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Harbor Books wants other teams' Pods kept off a group of nodes, while the payment Pods are allowed to run there. Which settings do that? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A taint repels Pods from a node, and a toleration on the payment Pods lets them be placed there. Tolerations belong to Pods and taints to nodes, never the other way round, and a priority does not exclude other Pods from a node.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. What is the difference between the taint effects No Schedule and No Execute? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. No Schedule stops new Pods that do not tolerate the taint, but leaves running Pods alone. No Execute also evicts running Pods that do not tolerate it. Prefer No Schedule is the soft version.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A Deployment's replicas must be spread across three zones, so that no zone holds more than one Pod more than the emptiest zone. Which setting does this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A topology spread constraint spreads matching Pods across domains, and max skew sets the largest allowed difference, here one, with the zone label as the topology key. A node selector would pin all replicas to one zone, and taints and priorities do not distribute Pods.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A node runs short of memory. Which Pods does the kube let evict first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Under node pressure the usual order is Best Effort Pods first, then Burstable ones, and Guaranteed Pods last. The kube let ranks by usage above requests and then priority, which gives this order in the usual case. Age and static Pods do not decide it.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Checkout Pods must keep running, even if less important batch Pods have to be evicted when the cluster is full. What gives them that ability? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A higher priority lets the scheduler preempt lower priority Pods to place the checkout Pods. A quota caps a namespace, a C P U limit does not change eviction order for the scheduler, and node name bypasses scheduling without freeing any room.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. The storefront H P A targets sixty percent average C P U utilization, but it never scales the Deployment. Which cause is likely? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. C P U utilization is measured against the Pods' requests, so with no request the H P A has nothing to compute, and takes no action. The update strategy, node labels and the Q O S class do not stop an H P A.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Pods stay Pending because no node has enough free C P U, and the cluster runs in a cloud. Which component adds nodes? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the number of nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled for lack of resources, and removes nodes that stay underutilized. The H P A changes Pod counts, and the V P A changes requests.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Which autoscaler sets the C P U and memory requests of a Pod from its observed usage? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The V P A sets requests from observed usage. The H P A changes the number of Pods, the Cluster Autoscaler changes the number of nodes, and KEDA scales workloads from events.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, D: filter, score, then bind. Question two, B: a taint on the nodes and a toleration on the Pods. Question three, A: No Execute also evicts running Pods. Question four, C: a topology spread constraint with max skew one. Question five, B: Best Effort Pods go first. Question six, D: a higher Priority Class allows preemption. Question seven, A: the H P A needs C P U requests. Question eight, C: the Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes. Question nine, A: the V P A sets requests from usage.
